subsection: 2. O'Connell after 1829, the Tithe War, the Poor Law and Young Ireland, 1830–1848

notes.h: Background: the Union, Emancipation and the parties
notes.b: O'Connell's career after 1829 only makes sense against the settlement he inherited. By 1830 he had won Catholic Emancipation and was now trying to use his popularity to change how Ireland was governed.
points: The Act of Union, in force from 1 January 1801, abolished the Irish Parliament, so Irish MPs sat at Westminster (the British Parliament in London) and Ireland was governed through Dublin Castle, the seat of the British administration.
The Church of Ireland was the established (state-supported) church, even though most Irish people were Catholic. This is why tithes, a tax for its clergy, became such a bitter grievance in the 1830s.

Catholic Emancipation came with the Roman Catholic Relief Act of 13 April 1829, which let Catholics sit in Parliament. It was won by O'Connell through the Catholic Association (founded 1823), the Catholic Rent (1824) and the Clare election of 1828.

The price of Emancipation was that the county franchise was raised to a £10 freehold, so the 40-shilling freeholders lost the vote. O'Connell, born near Cahersiveen, Co. Kerry, in 1775, was now known as 'the Liberator'.

Two British parties matter here. The Whigs were led by Earl Grey (prime minister 1830-34), Lord Melbourne (1835-41) and later Lord John Russell (from June 1846). The Tories, now called Conservatives, were led by Sir Robert Peel (prime minister 1841-46).
notes.tip: Examiners expect a comparison with the Emancipation campaign in any essay on O'Connell, so be ready to say that Emancipation succeeded where Repeal did not.

notes.h: O'Connell at Westminster and the Whig alliance, 1830-1841
notes.b: In the 1830s O'Connell led a group of Irish Repeal MPs at Westminster. Repeal (ending the Union and restoring an Irish Parliament under the Crown) got nowhere, so he worked with the Whigs to win practical reforms instead.
points: Re-elected unopposed for Clare in July 1829, O'Connell took his seat in the Commons in 1830 and gave up his legal practice. Supporters therefore funded him through an annual national collection, the O'Connell Tribute.

He supported Earl Grey's Whig government over parliamentary reform. The Irish Reform Act of 1832 raised Ireland's MPs from 100 to 105 but left the Irish electorate small, so it did little for most Catholics.
At the 1832 election about 40 MPs pledged to Repeal were returned, yet his Repeal motion of April 1834 was defeated by 523 votes to 38. This showed how little support Repeal had at Westminster.
The Lichfield House Compact (1835) was an informal bargain, not a written treaty. O'Connell and his MPs kept Lord Melbourne's Whigs in office in return for Irish reforms and fair appointments.

Under the Lord Lieutenant Lord Mulgrave, Chief Secretary Lord Morpeth and Under-Secretary Thomas Drummond (1835-1840), Catholics and liberals were appointed to office and stipendiary (paid, professional) magistrates were used. The police were centralised in the Irish Constabulary of 1836.

Drummond told the Tipperary magistrates in 1838 that "property has its duties as well as its rights", a warning to landlords that they could not expect the state to protect them without fulfilling their own obligations.

The Municipal Corporations (Ireland) Act 1840 abolished most of the closed Protestant town corporations (councils that chose their own members). About ten were reformed, with an elected council on a £10 householder franchise.

O'Connell became Lord Mayor of Dublin in 1841, the first Catholic to hold the office since the reign of James II. But the alliance won no Repeal and only limited tithe and municipal reform, so when Peel's Conservatives took office in 1841 he returned to agitation.
notes.tip: Know the Lichfield House Compact (1835) as an informal bargain and name Drummond, not Mulgrave, as the Under-Secretary; the Lord Lieutenant and the Under-Secretary are easily confused.

notes.h: The Tithe War: the grievance and the campaign, 1830-1834
notes.b: Tithe was a tax of about a tenth of agricultural produce, paid in money by the occupiers of land to support the clergy of the Church of Ireland, the church of a small minority. Catholics resented paying for a church they did not attend, and from 1830 they began to refuse.
points: The Tithe Composition Act of 1823 converted tithe in kind (a share of the crop) into fixed money payments. Money payments were harder to bear in bad years, which added to the resentment.
The campaign of non-payment began at Graiguenamanagh, Co. Kilkenny, in 1830-31. Farmers organised by the Catholic clergy refused to pay and protected each other's livestock from seizure.
Collectors (tithe proctors) and process servers seized cattle and goods for arrears, escorted by police and soldiers. Crowds gathered at the sound of horns and chapel bells to block them.
At Newtownbarry (Bunclody), Co. Wexford, in June 1831 yeomanry (part-time volunteer cavalry) fired on a crowd resisting a seizure and killed about a dozen people.
At Carrickshock, Co. Kilkenny, on 14 December 1831 a crowd attacked a process server and his police escort, killing the process server and about ten or eleven of the police.
At Gortroe near Rathcormac, Co. Cork, on 18 December 1834 soldiers fired on a crowd trying to stop a seizure from a widow, killing about twelve people.
The protest made tithe uncollectable in much of the south, so arrears mounted and the government had to advance money to clergy left without income.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Newtownbarry and Carrickshock (both 1831) with Gortroe/Rathcormac (1834), or the Tithe Composition Act (1823) with the Tithe Rentcharge Act (1838). Also say why Catholics resented tithe, not only what happened.

notes.h: The Tithe War: settlement and limits, 1834-1838
notes.b: After years of resistance the government could neither collect tithe nor ignore the problem. The delay came from a split inside the Whig party, and the final settlement changed who paid rather than whether tithe existed.
points: The Whigs split over appropriation, the idea of using surplus Church of Ireland revenues for non-religious purposes, which O'Connell supported. The disagreement delayed a settlement.

The Tithe Rentcharge Act (August 1838) cut the charge by about a quarter and made landlords responsible for paying it as part of the rent. This removed the direct clash between clergy and tenants, so the open conflict ended.
The settlement had limits: tithe was not abolished but moved into rent, and the Church of Ireland stayed established until disestablishment by the Irish Church Act of 1869 (in effect 1871).
notes.tip: In a Tithe War answer give a definition, where the campaign began, one or two dated clashes, the 1838 Act and what it left unsolved.

notes.b: Ireland was a very poor country, but before 1838 it had no national, rate-funded system of poor relief. The Whigs chose to copy England's workhouse system, even though an Irish commission had advised against it.
points: Before 1838 relief depended on charity, a few houses of industry (institutions for the poor) and county infirmaries, so most of the destitute had no reliable help.

A royal commission chaired by Richard Whately, the Church of Ireland Archbishop of Dublin (1833-1836), argued that Irish poverty was too widespread for workhouses. It recommended assisted emigration, public works and agricultural improvement.
The Whig government rejected the Whately report as too costly. It sent George Nicholls, an English poor law commissioner, who toured Ireland in 1836 and recommended workhouses on the English model.

The Irish Poor Law Act (July 1838) divided Ireland into 130 unions, each with a workhouse run by a board of guardians elected by ratepayers, with local magistrates sitting ex officio (automatically, because of their office).

Relief was given only inside the workhouse (indoor relief). Conditions were made deliberately harsher than the life of the poorest labourer so that only the truly destitute would apply, a rule known as the workhouse test.
Families were separated by sex and age on entry, inmates wore a uniform and worked, and admission carried a stigma, so the poor deeply resented the workhouse.
The cost was met by a poor rate on property, shared between landlord and occupier. From 1843 landlords paid the whole rate on holdings valued at under £4.

The workhouses held about 100,000 people in all and were designed for normal destitution, not mass famine. Most had opened only in the early 1840s, so the system was unready when the potato failed in 1845.
notes.tip: Name Nicholls (whose plan was adopted) over Whately (whose report was rejected), and explain why the 1838 system was not equal to the Famine. Do not confuse this Act with the Poor Law Extension Act of 1847.

notes.h: The Repeal campaign and Repeal Year, 1840-1843
notes.b: After the Whig alliance disappointed him, O'Connell turned to the method that had won Emancipation: peaceful mass pressure within the law, known as moral force. This time the aim was Repeal, and 1843 was to be the decisive year.
points: O'Connell founded the Repeal Association in April 1840, with a Repeal Rent of a penny a month. It was modelled on the Catholic Rent, so even the poorest could join and the movement had money.
Repeal meant restoring a separate Irish Parliament under the Crown, not separation from Britain. O'Connell often hinted he would accept a federal compromise or substantial reform instead.
Support grew slowly until Dublin Corporation, led by O'Connell, debated Repeal in early 1843. He then declared 1843 Repeal Year.
The Catholic clergy again acted as local organisers. Father Theobald Mathew's temperance movement, though separate, supplied disciplined crowds and bands.
About forty monster meetings were held in 1843, mostly on sites with historic associations such as Tara, Mullaghmast (1 October) and Clontarf, to give Repeal a sense of Irish history.
The largest was at the Hill of Tara on 15 August 1843; supporters claimed up to a million attended. The Nation newspaper publicised the meetings and gave the campaign a younger, more militant tone.
In May 1843 Peel told the Commons that he would risk any alternative, even war, rather than see the empire dismembered. The government dismissed Repeal magistrates and sent reinforcements to Ireland.
notes.tip: For a short paragraph on Repeal give the 1840 founding, the Rent, the clergy, about forty monster meetings including Tara, Clontarf, arrest and the outcome, with dates.

notes.h: Clontarf, the state trial and the decline of Repeal, 1843-1847
notes.b: Peel called O'Connell's bluff at Clontarf, and the movement never recovered. The sequence from the ban to the Famine shows why a leader who would not go beyond the law could not force the government's hand.
points: The government banned the monster meeting called for Clontarf on 8 October 1843 only on the evening before (7 October), and troops and artillery occupied the site. Do not confuse this with the medieval battle of Clontarf.
O'Connell cancelled the meeting and sent people home, fearing a massacre. This preserved his moral force policy but exposed the fact that he would not go beyond the law.
He and other leaders, including Charles Gavan Duffy, were arrested in October 1843 and convicted of conspiracy in 1844 by a jury from which Catholics had been excluded.
He was sentenced to a year in prison and a £2,000 fine. He spent about three months in the Richmond Bridewell before the House of Lords quashed the verdict in September 1844.

Peel combined coercion with conciliation: the Devon Commission on land (1843), the Charitable Bequests Act (1844), a larger Maynooth College grant (1845) and the Queen's Colleges (1845). These offered Catholics concessions, so Repeal lost some of its force.
O'Connell was 68 in 1843, and after prison his energy and health declined. He proposed a federal alternative in 1844, which confused supporters because it seemed to give up full Repeal.

From 1845 the Famine, which began when potato blight was first reported that year, destroyed the Repeal Rent and the mass following. O'Connell renewed his alliance with the Whigs when Lord John Russell took office in 1846.

Why Repeal failed: both British parties, Parliament and Protestant Ulster opposed it, and Peel called O'Connell's bluff at Clontarf. Within the movement, it was overwhelmingly Catholic, and the Famine and the Young Ireland split followed.
notes.tip: A strong answer on why Repeal failed pairs external causes (both British parties, Peel's firmness, Protestant Ulster) with internal ones (reliance on bluff, ill health, the Young Ireland split, the Famine). Naming the cancellation of Clontarf as the turning point earns credit.

notes.b: Young Ireland was a group of mostly young, middle-class writers within the Repeal movement. They developed a cultural idea of the Irish nation, meaning a people bound by shared history, culture and language rather than by religion.
points: Charles Gavan Duffy, a Catholic journalist from Co. Monaghan, Thomas Davis, a Protestant barrister from Mallow, and John Blake Dillon, a Catholic barrister, founded The Nation, first published on 15 October 1842.

The Nation became one of the most widely read papers in Ireland, passed from hand to hand and read aloud in reading rooms, so its reach was far greater than its sales. It published history, ballads and essays.
Its idea of nationality was cultural and non-sectarian: a nation shared history, culture and, ideally, the Irish language, and included Protestants as well as Catholics.
The Library of Ireland, a series of cheap books on Irish history and literature launched by Duffy in 1845, extended the paper's educational work.

Young Ireland disagreed with O'Connell over federalism (1844), over his alliance with the Whigs, and over the Queen's Colleges (1845), which Davis welcomed as mixed education and O'Connell condemned as godless.
The final break came over the peace resolutions of July 1846, which O'Connell proposed so that the Association would declare the use of force never justified, clearing the way for his Whig alliance.

Thomas Francis Meagher's Sword Speech (28 July 1846) refused to condemn force in all circumstances, and Young Ireland walked out of the Repeal Association. Meagher's speech is not to be confused with the peace resolutions it answered.
notes.tip: State the cultural, non-sectarian idea of the nation first, then The Nation, then the split and 1848. Keep the peace resolutions (O'Connell's motion) distinct from the Sword Speech (Meagher's reply).

notes.h: The Irish Confederation and the build-up to 1848
notes.b: Having left the Association, the Young Irelanders organised on their own. Events in Europe and a harsher government response pushed them from argument towards rebellion, and this readiness to use force is what is meant by physical force republicanism.
points: The Young Irelanders founded the Irish Confederation in January 1847, led by William Smith O'Brien, a Protestant landowner and MP, with Duffy and Meagher.

James Fintan Lalor argued in The Nation that the land question should be linked to national independence, so that tenants' grievances would drive the national cause. This idea influenced John Mitchel.
Mitchel broke with the Confederation's moderates and founded the United Irishman in February 1848 to preach open revolution. He urged tenants to refuse rent and resist food exports.
The overthrow of Louis Philippe in Paris in February 1848 encouraged the Confederates to plan a rising, and Smith O'Brien and Meagher went to Paris with an address of support.

Mitchel was convicted under the new Treason Felony Act (April 1848) in May 1848 and transported for fourteen years. In July 1848 the government suspended habeas corpus, the right not to be held without trial, forcing the leaders into a hasty rising.
notes.tip: Smith O'Brien led in 1848; Mitchel, the revolutionary journalist, had already been transported before the rising.

notes.h: Ballingarry, 1848, and the legacy of Young Ireland
notes.b: The 1848 rising was small and quickly over, but it mattered for what it passed on. It linked Young Ireland to the physical force tradition (the belief that independence needs armed rebellion) later taken up by the Fenians.
points: On 29 July 1848 Smith O'Brien's small band besieged police in the Widow McCormack's house at Ballingarry, Co. Tipperary. About two rebels were killed and the rest dispersed.

Reasons for failure: no preparation or weapons, a starving and demoralised population, strong opposition from the Catholic clergy, government foreknowledge, and leaders who would not risk lives or property.

Smith O'Brien, Meagher, Terence MacManus and Patrick O'Donohoe were sentenced to death at Clonmel in 1848. The sentences were commuted (reduced) to transportation to Van Diemen's Land, while Dillon escaped to America.

James Stephens, wounded at Ballingarry, and John O'Mahony, who also took part in the rising, escaped to France. They later founded the Fenian movement, so 1848 became a link in the physical force tradition.
Young Ireland's other legacy was cultural: The Nation, the Library of Ireland and the ballads shaped the later idea of the Irish nation.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Ballingarry 1848 (Young Ireland) with the Fenian rising of 1867. Name Stephens and O'Mahony to show the physical force link.

notes.b: O'Connell, a barrister born in Co. Kerry in 1775 and known as the Liberator, spent his last seventeen years trying to turn the mass movement that won Emancipation into political change. The years covered here are 1830-47 only.
points: Aims after 1829: Repeal of the Union, the end of tithes, municipal reform, fair government and a share of office for Catholics, all by constitutional means (moral force).
Participant: he led the Irish party at Westminster, made the Lichfield House Compact, founded the Repeal Association, called Repeal Year and decided to cancel Clontarf.
He was shaped by events as much as he shaped them: Peel's firmness in 1843, the Famine from 1845 and Young Ireland's challenge set the limits of what he could achieve.

Strengths, for example: an unrivalled orator and organiser, master of peaceful mass agitation, skilled parliamentarian and lawyer, and committed to religious liberty for all, including Jews and dissenters, and to the abolition of slavery.

Weaknesses, such as his reliance on bluff, his willingness to drop Repeal for Whig favours, rigid control of the movement, the patronage given to his family, and a Catholic-centred movement that alienated Protestants.
He died at Genoa on 15 May 1847 on his way to Rome. His heart was buried in Rome and his body in Glasnevin Cemetery, Dublin.
Contemporaries: to Catholic Ireland he was the Liberator; to the Times and British Tories he was a dangerous agitator; to Young Ireland in 1846 he was a tired leader who had sold Repeal to the Whigs.

Historians: Oliver MacDonagh, in a two-volume biography (1988 and 1989), sees him as a founder of mass democratic politics. Critics note that Repeal failed and that his movement deepened the link between Catholicism and nationalism.
notes.tip: The commonest Higher essay asks for strengths and weaknesses, why Repeal failed or how far his leadership explains success and failure. State a clear judgement at the start and back it with dated evidence: the Compact (1835), the Repeal Association (1840), Repeal Year and Clontarf (1843). A list of events with no verdict scores poorly.

notes.b: Davis was the thinker of Young Ireland. He was a witness to and participant in the Repeal movement through ideas and writing rather than a political leader, and he died before the Famine and the split.
points: Born on 14 October 1814 in Mallow, Co. Cork, the son of an army surgeon, Davis was a Protestant who studied at Trinity College Dublin and was called to the bar in 1838.
He joined the Repeal Association in 1841 and co-founded The Nation in 1842, becoming its leading writer.

His essays argued for a nationality above religion, for the Irish language, for Irish history and for self-reliance. He wrote in 1843 that "a people without a language of its own is only half a nation".
His ballads, including A Nation Once Again and The West's Asleep, made romantic nationalism popular among the young.
He backed mixed, non-denominational education and welcomed the Queen's Colleges in 1845, which led to a bitter public clash with O'Connell.
He died of scarlet fever on 16 September 1845, aged 30, before the Famine took hold and before the peace resolutions split the movement. He never saw the split or the rising.

He shaped the movement through ideas, and was shaped by it: O'Connell's Repeal Association gave him a platform, but his secular views brought him into conflict with it. Contemporaries such as Duffy, his friend, revered him as the soul of Young Ireland, while O'Connell's Catholic supporters distrusted his mixed-education views.
Historians see him as the founder of cultural nationalism, whose ideas the Gaelic League generation drew on, and note that his ideal of a nation uniting Protestant and Catholic was never realised.
notes.tip: For a profile of Davis give his background, joining the Repeal Association, founding The Nation, his ideas on nationality and language, his ballads, the Queen's Colleges clash and his early death. Each correct dated point earns marks. Davis and Meagher are different men.

notes.h: Assessment: O'Connell and Young Ireland, achievements and limits
notes.b: Examiners reward a clear verdict. The achievements and limits below are paired so each can be turned into a judgement.
points: O'Connell's achievement: he created mass constitutional politics, won practical reforms with the Whigs and gave Irish Catholics political confidence.
O'Connell's limit: Repeal, his central aim after 1829, failed completely, and the movement collapsed after Clontarf, his ill health and the Famine.
Tithe War achievement: popular resistance forced the 1838 settlement. Limit: tithe was only shifted into rent, and the established Church survived until 1869.
Poor Law achievement: Ireland gained a national relief system and local elected boards. Limit: the workhouse model failed when the Famine created mass rather than individual destitution.
Young Ireland's achievement: The Nation created a cultural, non-sectarian idea of the nation and a body of history and ballads that shaped later nationalism.
Young Ireland's limit: it split the national movement in 1846, its rising of 1848 was a fiasco, and its non-sectarian ideal won few Protestants.

Contemporary and later views: to Catholic Ireland O'Connell was the Liberator but Young Ireland saw a tired leader; Davis was revered by Duffy, while historians now see him as the founder of cultural nationalism.

Contribution to nationalism: O'Connell left the constitutional tradition later taken up by Butt and Parnell; Young Ireland left the cultural and physical force traditions taken up by the Fenians and the Gaelic revival.
notes.tip: Compare Young Ireland with O'Connell, or with the Fenians, by giving the difference in methods and ideas and a clear point on what each contributed. Weaker answers confuse 1848 with 1867.

keyTerms.definition: A people bound together by shared history, culture and language rather than by religion, the idea of Irish nationality that Thomas Davis and The Nation promoted from 1842.
The belief that Irish independence could be won only by armed rebellion; Young Ireland's refusal to rule out force in 1846 and the 1848 rising passed this tradition to the Fenians.
O'Connell's aim of dissolving the Union and restoring an Irish Parliament under the Crown, campaigned for by the Repeal Association from 1840.
A tax on the occupiers of land, paid to support the Church of Ireland clergy, whose collection caused the Tithe War of the 1830s.
The informal agreement of 1835 in which O'Connell's MPs supported the Whig government in return for Irish reforms and fair appointments.
One of the huge open-air Repeal rallies of 1843, held at historic sites such as Tara, to show the strength of popular support.
Resolutions O'Connell put to the Repeal Association in July 1846 declaring the use of force never justified, which caused the Young Ireland walk-out.
The Poor Law principle that relief should be given only inside a workhouse whose conditions were harsher than the worst outside, so only the destitute would apply.
The body, elected by ratepayers with ex officio magistrates, that ran each poor law union's workhouse and set the poor rate.
Nationalism based on a distinctive history, literature and language, promoted by Young Ireland through The Nation.

factCards.definition: The Lichfield House Compact and Whig reforms (1835–1840), municipal reform and his election as Lord Mayor of Dublin (1841), and the mass Repeal movement of 1843.
Both British parties and Protestant Ulster opposed it, Peel called his bluff at Clontarf, he would not use force, and his health, the Famine and the Young Ireland split ended the movement.
He co-founded The Nation (1842), defined a non-sectarian cultural nationalism that valued the Irish language, and wrote popular ballads such as A Nation Once Again.
O'Connell's MPs kept Melbourne's Whigs in power in return for reforms, including Drummond's fair administration and municipal reform in 1840.
Peel's government banned the meeting set for 8 October 1843; O'Connell called it off, was arrested, convicted of conspiracy in 1844 and freed on appeal to the Lords.
Newtownbarry, Co. Wexford (June 1831), Carrickshock, Co. Kilkenny (December 1831) and Gortroe near Rathcormac, Co. Cork (December 1834).
It cut tithe by about a quarter and made landlords pay it as part of the rent, ending the Tithe War.
